what: A message queue holds jobs between the service that creates them and the workers that do them. The sender drops a message in and moves on; a worker picks it up later and deletes it when done.
like: Like a ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen: waiters clip orders on and go back to tables, and cooks take the next ticket when ready.
why: Fast responses: slow work happens in the background, not in the request
Absorbs traffic spikes: the queue grows and workers catch up at their own pace
Decouples services: if workers are down, messages wait instead of being lost

nodes.t: Dead letter queue|after too many tries

steps.d: The web service puts a small message, like resize photo 42, on the queue and replies to the user straight away. Big files go to storage, with only a link in the message.
A worker pulls the message. In SQS it is now hidden from other workers for the visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default, while the work happens.
When the job succeeds the worker deletes it (SQS) or sends an ack (RabbitMQ). It first checks the message ID, so a repeat delivery does no harm.
If the worker crashes or runs past the timeout, the message becomes visible again and another worker retries it. That is at-least-once delivery.
After maxReceiveCount receives without success, the message moves to a dead letter queue, so one broken message cannot block the rest. An alarm tells you to look.
Queue length is your backpressure signal. When it grows, add workers; when it shrinks, remove them. Prefetch limits stop any one worker grabbing too much.

numbers.l: default SQS visibility timeout; the maximum is 12 hours
default SQS message retention, adjustable from 1 minute to 14 days
largest SQS message; store bigger payloads in S3
SQS FIFO messages per API method, batching 10 per call
in-flight messages allowed on an SQS standard queue

choices.d: Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once, best-effort order. FIFO: order kept per message group and duplicate sends removed within 5 minutes, but lower throughput.
Set it longer than a normal job takes. For jobs of unknown length, start short and extend with ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat while working.

Pick maxReceiveCount high enough to ride out brief hiccups; 1 sends a message aside after one failure. Give the DLQ a longer retention than the main queue so failed messages are still there to inspect.
Use manual acks, since automatic acks count a message done the moment it is sent. In RabbitMQ a prefetch of 100 to 300 usually gives good throughput.
Give every message a unique ID and record processed IDs, or make the action safe to repeat, like set status=paid rather than add 10 pounds.

instead.why: Replayable log with many reader groups and very high throughput
One event delivered to many different services at once
Lightweight list or stream queue when you already run Redis

breaks.d: Messages arrive faster than workers finish them.
breaks.see: Queue depth and age of the oldest message climbing
breaks.fix: Autoscale workers on queue depth, speed up the handler, batch receives

breaks.d: A worker finished but its delete or ack was lost, so the message came back.
breaks.see: Duplicate emails or charges for one message ID
breaks.fix: Idempotent consumers: store processed IDs, or use FIFO deduplication on send

breaks.d: Jobs take longer than the visibility timeout, so a second worker starts the same job.
breaks.see: Receive count above 1 on healthy messages; overlapping work in logs
breaks.fix: Raise the timeout, or extend it with a heartbeat during long jobs

breaks.d: One message always fails, maybe bad data, and keeps being retried.
breaks.see: The same message ID failing again and again in logs
breaks.fix: A DLQ with a sensible maxReceiveCount, plus an alarm and a redrive after fixing

breaks.d: A standard queue does not promise order, so updates can apply out of sequence.
breaks.see: An older update overwriting a newer one
breaks.fix: FIFO with a message group per entity, or version numbers on each update

say: The API puts a job on a queue and returns 202 straight away, and a pool of workers processes jobs in the background.
Delivery is at-least-once, so every handler is idempotent, keyed on a message ID we store when the job completes.
Failed jobs retry through the visibility timeout, and after a few attempts they land in a dead letter queue with an alarm on it.
We autoscale workers on queue depth, so a traffic spike makes the queue longer for a while instead of overloading the database.

followups.q: Why not just call the other service directly?
followups.a: A direct call means the user waits for the slow work, and if the other service is down the request fails. A queue lets you reply fast, smooths spikes and keeps work safe until a worker is free.

followups.q: How do you get exactly-once processing?
followups.a: Delivery is usually at-least-once, so aim for exactly-once effect: idempotent handlers that record each message ID, or update in the same database transaction. SQS FIFO also drops duplicate sends within a 5 minute window.
Use FIFO with a message group ID per customer or order. Order holds inside each group while different groups run in parallel. A standard queue gives only best-effort order.

followups.q: A worker crashes mid-job. What happens?
followups.a: It never deleted or acked the message, so after the visibility timeout (SQS) or when its connection closes (RabbitMQ) the message is delivered again, marked as a redelivery, to another worker.

today: In August 2025 Amazon SQS raised its largest message from 256 KiB to 1 MiB, so many payloads no longer need the store-in-S3-and-send-a-link pattern.

check.q: A worker takes the message but crashes before deleting it. What does SQS do?
check.a: Makes it visible again after the visibility timeout
d: Sends it to the DLQ at once
check.why: The message comes back so another worker can retry it - that is at-least-once delivery.

check.q: Why must queue consumers be idempotent?
check.a: The same message can be delivered more than once
d: It removes the need for acks
check.why: Retries and lost acks cause repeats, so handling a message twice must be safe.

check.q: One bad message fails every time. What stops it retrying forever?
check.a: A dead letter queue with maxReceiveCount
check.why: After that many receives the message moves aside to the DLQ for a look.

check.q: You need a customer's updates applied in order. Which setup?
check.a: A FIFO queue with the customer ID as message group
d: A standard queue with more workers
check.why: FIFO keeps order inside each message group while other customers run in parallel.
